title: Anti-Patterns & Singleton Pitfalls: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on the classic design anti-patterns (God object, spaghetti code, golden hammer, premature abstraction), then singleton as global state, the four thread-safe singleton implementations, and why singletons hurt testing.

chapters.title: Anti-Patterns Mental Model
points: Anti-pattern = a common 'solution' that looks reasonable but causes recurring harm; each one has a symptom, a cause and a refactor
God object: one class that knows or does too much (e.g. UserManager does auth, email, billing, DB); symptoms are thousands of lines, many unrelated fields and every change touching it
Spaghetti code: tangled control flow with no clear structure (deep nesting, goto-style jumps, shared mutable state, long methods); you cannot trace what calls what
Golden hammer: using one familiar tool or pattern for every problem ('when all you have is a hammer'), e.g. a relational DB or Singleton or microservices for everything
Premature abstraction: building interfaces, factories or generics before a second real use exists; guess-shaped abstractions are wrong shaped and cost more than duplication

chapters.title: Fixing the Four Anti-Patterns
points: Fix God object: split by responsibility (Single Responsibility Principle), extract classes like AuthService, Mailer, BillingService, and inject them rather than hard-wiring
Fix spaghetti: extract small functions, use guard clauses to cut nesting, separate layers (UI / logic / data) and remove shared mutable state; add tests first so refactor is safe
Fix golden hammer: choose the tool from the requirements and trade-offs, compare at least two options, and ask 'what problem is this pattern actually solving here?'
Fix premature abstraction: apply the Rule of Three (duplicate twice, abstract on the third) and YAGNI; wrong abstraction is costlier than duplication, so inline it back and re-extract
Comparison of cause vs signal: God object = too many responsibilities, spaghetti = tangled flow, golden hammer = wrong tool choice, premature abstraction = speculative structure

chapters.title: Singleton as Global State
points: Singleton = private constructor + static getInstance() so one instance exists per JVM (per class loader) with a global access point
Hidden dependency: callers use Config.getInstance() inside methods, so the constructor/signature does not reveal what the class needs
Shared mutable state: any code can change the singleton, giving order-dependent bugs, action-at-a-distance and race conditions across threads
Singleton violates SRP (manages its own lifecycle and does business work) and tightly couples every caller to the concrete class
Better alternative: create one instance at the composition root and pass it in via dependency injection; 'single instance' is a lifetime choice, not a global access point

chapters.title: Thread-Safe Singleton Implementations
points: Eager initialization: private static final Foo INSTANCE = new Foo(); thread-safe via class loading, simple, but created even if never used and cannot catch exceptions lazily
Synchronized getInstance(): correct and lazy but every call takes the lock, which is slow on the hot path

Double-checked locking: check null, synchronized(Foo.class), check null again, then create; the field MUST be volatile, otherwise reordering can publish a partially constructed object (needs Java 5+ memory model)

Holder idiom: private static class Holder { static final Foo INSTANCE = new Foo(); } with getInstance() returning Holder.INSTANCE; lazy, lock-free, safe because JVM class initialization is thread-safe

Enum singleton: enum Foo { INSTANCE; } is the most robust (Effective Java); safe against reflection and serialization attacks and thread-safe, but cannot extend a class and is eagerly loaded with the enum

chapters.title: Testing Problems with Singletons
points: State leaks between tests: a singleton keeps its state for the whole JVM, so test A's changes break test B and results depend on execution order
Cannot substitute a mock: code calling Foo.getInstance() is hard-wired, so you cannot stub the database, clock or mailer without PowerMock or reflection hacks
Parallel tests collide: shared mutable singleton state makes parallel test runs flaky and non-deterministic
Workarounds are smells: adding reset() or a setInstance() method just for tests weakens the design; fix it by extracting an interface and injecting it through the constructor
Testable design: depend on an interface, inject a fake in tests, and let the app wire the one real instance at startup (Spring singleton scope is one bean per container, not a global)

chapters.title: Anti-Patterns and Singleton Cheat Sheet
points: Smell to fix map: God object -> split by SRP; spaghetti -> small functions plus layers; golden hammer -> pick tool by requirement; premature abstraction -> Rule of Three
Singleton recipe table: eager (simple, not lazy), synchronized (lazy, slow), DCL + volatile (lazy, fast, tricky), holder (lazy, lock-free, preferred), enum (safest, no inheritance)
DCL checklist: private static volatile Foo instance; if (instance == null) { synchronized (Foo.class) { if (instance == null) instance = new Foo(); } }
Singleton testing rule: no static getInstance() in business code; inject an interface via the constructor
Interview Point: Why must DCL use volatile? Why prefer the holder or enum over DCL? How do you test code that uses a singleton?
